title: Bipolar disorder
blurb: Tell mania from hypomania, manage an acute manic episode with NICE CG185 and plan long-term relapse prevention.
question: Olivia, 29, with bipolar disorder, has slept 2 hours a night for 5 days, has spent £8,000 on a new business idea and talks rapidly without pause. She takes sertraline and no other medication. What should happen to her medication?

teach.body: Bipolar disorder is a long-term condition with episodes of high mood (mania or hypomania) and low mood (depression), usually with periods of stable mood in between. High moods can be severe (mania) or milder (hypomania). In plain English: mood swings far beyond ordinary ups and downs, lasting days or weeks, that can damage health, money, relationships and safety. NICE CG185 covers bipolar I, bipolar II, mixed states and rapid cycling.

head: Area
What you may see
rows: Racing thoughts, fast and pressured speech

steps.label: Calm, low-stimulus setting
steps.sub: Advise no big decisions until recovered (1.5.1)

steps.label: Not enough?
steps.sub: Alternative antipsychotic, then consider adding lithium (1.5.4-1.5.5)

teach.caption: Already on lithium: check the level and consider adding an antipsychotic (1.5.8). Do not offer lamotrigine to treat mania (1.5.12).

teach.body: After each episode, discuss long-term management. NICE says offer lithium as the first-line, long-term treatment, explaining it is the most effective for preventing relapse. If lithium is ineffective, poorly tolerated or unsuitable (for example the person will not have blood tests), consider an antipsychotic. Valproate has strict MHRA restrictions in people under 55. Offer a structured psychological intervention designed for bipolar disorder to prevent relapse.

items.label: Trigger: stress, lost sleep, shift work

teach.caption: Each person's signs differ. CG185 1.4.1: a jointly agreed plan names triggers, early warning signs and what to do, including medication steps agreed in advance.

teach.body: NICE asks for a risk management plan written with the person and, if possible, their carer: personal triggers and early warning signs, the person's own coping strategies, any agreed medication increase, who to contact in a crisis, and how primary and secondary care will respond. The person and GP get copies. Risk areas include self-neglect, self-harm, suicide, risks to others, driving, spending and sexual vulnerability.

Olivia's reduced sleep, overspending and pressured speech suggest mania. On the ward Nurse Clarke offers a quiet room and reduced stimulation, and gently advises her to postpone business decisions. The team considers stopping the sertraline and offers an antipsychotic such as olanzapine, discussing side effects with her. Nurse Clarke assesses financial and sexual vulnerability, involves her partner with consent, and later builds her relapse signature into a crisis plan.

teach.text: Do not keep an antidepressant running in mania; NICE says consider stopping it. Do not use lamotrigine for mania (it is for bipolar depression). And lithium, not valproate, is the first-line long-term choice.

items: Mania is severe high mood; hypomania is milder.
Acute mania: calm environment, consider stopping antidepressants, offer haloperidol, olanzapine, quetiapine or risperidone.
Already on lithium: check the level and consider adding an antipsychotic.
Lithium is first-line long term; lamotrigine is not for mania.
Joint crisis plan: triggers, early warning signs, coping, medication steps, contacts.

summary: You can now distinguish mania from hypomania and manage acute mania in line with NICE CG185. You can plan long-term treatment with lithium first line and build a relapse signature into a crisis plan.

A.q: Which medication does NICE recommend as the first-line long-term treatment for bipolar disorder?
A.why: CG185 1.7.7: offer lithium as a first-line, long-term pharmacological treatment for bipolar disorder.

whyNot.1: Valproate is not first line and has MHRA restrictions in people under 55.
whyNot.2: Lamotrigine has a role in bipolar depression, not as first-line long-term treatment.
whyNot.3: An antidepressant is not a long-term mood stabiliser and can destabilise mood.

A.q: What best describes the difference between hypomania and mania?
options: Hypomania is a milder high mood
Hypomania is a mixed affective state
A.why: NHS: high moods in bipolar disorder can be severe (mania) or mild (hypomania).

whyNot.1: Hypomania lasts at least 4 days and mania at least a week; neither is defined by lasting several months.
whyNot.3: A mixed state has both manic and depressive symptoms (CG185 1.5.11).

A.q: Which drug does NICE CG185 say should NOT be offered to treat mania?
A.why: CG185 1.5.12: do not offer lamotrigine to treat mania. Haloperidol, olanzapine, quetiapine and risperidone are the recommended antipsychotics (1.5.3).

whyNot.0: Quetiapine is one of the antipsychotics NICE lists for mania.
whyNot.1: Haloperidol is one of the antipsychotics NICE lists for mania.
whyNot.2: Risperidone is one of the antipsychotics NICE lists for mania.

B.q: Raj, 35, develops mania while taking fluoxetine as his only medication. What does NICE recommend?
options: Increase fluoxetine to treat the mood instability
Consider stopping it and offer an antipsychotic
Add valproate as the first-choice drug
B.why: CG185 1.5.2: if mania develops on antidepressant monotherapy, consider stopping the antidepressant and offer an antipsychotic whether or not it is stopped.

whyNot.0: Increasing an antidepressant may worsen mania.
whyNot.2: Lamotrigine should not be offered for mania.
whyNot.3: Valproate is not first choice and is restricted under 55.

B.q: Helen, 50, on lithium for years, becomes manic. What should be done first, according to NICE?
options: Add an SSRI to stabilise mood
B.why: CG185 1.5.8: if already taking lithium, check plasma lithium levels to optimise treatment, and consider adding an antipsychotic.

whyNot.0: Stopping lithium abruptly risks rebound and valproate is restricted.
whyNot.3: Antidepressants are not used to treat mania.

B.q: Gary, 41, is manic on the ward and wants to sign a contract to sell his house today. What is the most appropriate nursing advice?
options: Help him complete it so he feels respected
Tell him the sale is not allowed while admitted
Ask his solicitor to cancel any future sale
Advise him to delay big decisions until well
B.why: CG185 1.5.1: advise people with mania or hypomania not to make important decisions until they have recovered, and support a calm environment.

whyNot.0: Supporting an impulsive major decision during mania risks serious harm.
whyNot.1: Admission does not legally bar him; advice and support are the response.
whyNot.2: Contacting his solicitor without consent breaches confidentiality.

C.q: Ana, 32, has recovered from mania treated with olanzapine. She is deciding on long-term treatment. What should the nurse explain?
options: Long-term treatment is not needed after one episode
Valproate is the preferred drug in women of her age
Lamotrigine is the best choice to prevent new mania
Lithium is the most effective at preventing relapse
C.why: CG185 1.7.5-1.7.7: discuss continuing what worked or switching to lithium, explaining lithium is the most effective long-term treatment; offer lithium first line.

whyNot.0: NICE asks for a long-term management discussion after each episode.
whyNot.1: Valproate is restricted in women able to have children.
whyNot.2: NICE says do not offer lamotrigine to treat mania (1.5.12); lithium, not lamotrigine, is named the most effective long-term treatment (1.7.5).

C.q: Simon, 38, has bipolar disorder and is being discharged to his GP. Which element must his care plan include under NICE CG185?
options: A ban on any travel abroad for 6 months
Weekly lithium levels for the first year
A crisis plan with his early warning signs
Medication supervised daily by his family
C.why: CG185 1.9.4: the plan includes recovery goals, a crisis plan with early warning symptoms and triggers of mania and depression, a mental state assessment and a medication plan.

whyNot.0: Travel bans are not part of NICE care planning.
whyNot.1: Weekly levels are for starting or changing dose, not stable maintenance.
whyNot.3: Supervision by family is not a NICE requirement.

C.q: Priya, 27, with bipolar disorder, notices she is sleeping 4 hours and feels full of energy, which happened before her last two manic episodes. What is the best first step under her agreed plan?
options: Wait for spending or fast speech to appear first
Follow her agreed plan and contact her team
Stop all medication to see if mood settles
Go to A&E and ask to be detained there
C.why: CG185 1.4.1: the risk plan sets out early warning signs and a protocol for the person's coping strategies, possible medication changes agreed in advance, and who to contact.

whyNot.0: Waiting loses the chance to act early on her relapse signature.
whyNot.3: Early warning signs call for the agreed plan, not emergency detention.

reteach.title: Spot the high early
reteach.question: What matters most in caring for someone with bipolar disorder?

blocks.h: Early signs, right drug, shared plan
blocks.body: Sleep loss is often the first sign of a high. In mania: calm environment, consider stopping antidepressants, offer an antipsychotic. Long term: lithium first line. Write a crisis plan with the person that names their own early warning signs and what to do.

explain.body: Elated or irritable mood, little need for sleep, racing thoughts, fast speech, overconfidence, impulsive spending and risk-taking; in mania sometimes delusions or hallucinations.

test.q: Which change is often an early warning sign of a manic relapse?
test.why: Reduced need for sleep is a typical feature of high mood and often an early warning sign (NHS; CG185 1.4.1).

whyNot.0: Oversleeping is more typical of depression.

explain.body: Not on an antipsychotic or mood stabiliser: offer haloperidol, olanzapine, quetiapine or risperidone. If poorly tolerated or ineffective, try another from the list; then consider adding lithium.

test.q: Which group lists the antipsychotics NICE names for treating mania?
test.why: CG185 1.5.3: offer haloperidol, olanzapine, quetiapine or risperidone.

whyNot.0: Clozapine and others in this list are not the CG185 mania options.
whyNot.2: Clozapine and sulpiride are not the CG185 mania options.
whyNot.3: These are not the CG185 mania options.

explain.body: Lithium first line. If unsuitable, an antipsychotic such as aripiprazole, olanzapine, quetiapine or risperidone. Valproate combinations later, under MHRA rules. Offer a structured psychological intervention to prevent relapse.

test.q: Lithium is unsuitable for Mark because he refuses regular blood tests. What does NICE suggest considering for long-term treatment?
options: Lamotrigine on its own for mania
An SSRI on its own long term
test.why: CG185 1.7.8: if lithium is ineffective, poorly tolerated or unsuitable (for example the person does not agree to blood monitoring), consider an antipsychotic.

whyNot.1: NICE says do not offer lamotrigine for mania (1.5.12), and it is not among the 1.7.8 options when lithium is unsuitable.
whyNot.2: An antidepressant alone can trigger mania.
whyNot.3: NICE offers alternatives rather than no treatment by default.

explain.body: Written jointly with the person and carer: triggers, early warning signs, coping strategies, any agreed medication increase, crisis contacts, and agreed primary and secondary care responses. Copies to the person and GP.

test.q: Who should receive a copy of the risk management plan, according to NICE CG185?
test.why: CG185 1.4.1: give the person and their GP a copy of the plan, and encourage the person to share it with carers.

whyNot.0: Sharing with police or employers is not part of the plan and breaches confidentiality.
whyNot.1: These organisations do not receive the clinical plan.
whyNot.2: NICE names the person and GP as recipients.
